milestones.title: Chen Lai-chang patent opens the Taipei Basin
milestones.detail: A partnership of settlers from Quanzhou obtains a patent to reclaim Dajiala, an area covering Bangka, Dadaocheng and the later city centre. The basin had been home to the Ketagalan people.

milestones.title: Tamsui Subprefecture brings Qing administration
milestones.detail: After the Zhu Yigui rebellion the Qing court creates Tamsui Subprefecture for the land north of the Dajia River, putting the Taipei area under Chinese administration for the first time.

milestones.title: Lungshan Temple built in Bangka
milestones.detail: Settlers from Quanzhou build Lungshan Temple in Bangka, the river port that becomes northern Taiwan's main town.

milestones.title: Bangka becomes the seat of local government
milestones.detail: The assistant magistrate's office moves from Xinzhuang to Bangka. The town, with four to five thousand households and shops, is counted as Taiwan's third town and the largest in the north.
milestones.source: https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/臺北市歷史 (citing 姚瑩, 臺北道里記)

milestones.title: Feud drives traders to found Dadaocheng
milestones.detail: After fighting between rival immigrant groups in Bangka, the Tong'an people move a few kilometres north to Dadaocheng. As Bangka's harbour silts up, Dadaocheng becomes the trading centre of northern Taiwan.

milestones.title: Taipeh Prefecture created
milestones.detail: The Qing court approves a new prefecture for northern Taiwan. Its capital is laid out on open fields between Bangka and Dadaocheng.

milestones.title: City walls completed
milestones.detail: The walls of Taipei, begun in 1882, are finished in 1884. Nearly five kilometres long with five gates, they enclose about one square kilometre of offices and temples.

milestones.title: Capital of the new Taiwan Province
milestones.detail: Taiwan is declared a province and its government is placed, provisionally, at Taipeh. Governor Liu Mingchuan paves streets, installs electric lighting and builds a railway to Keelung.

milestones.title: Japanese rule begins; Taihoku the colonial capital
milestones.detail: China cedes Taiwan to Japan. Japanese troops enter Taipei on 7 June 1895 and the Government-General is installed there.

milestones.title: Walls demolished for boulevards
milestones.detail: Under the urban improvement plan of 1900 the Government-General begins pulling down the city walls. Through roads join the walled city, Bangka and Dadaocheng into one town.

milestones.title: Taihoku City incorporated
milestones.detail: Taihoku is incorporated as a city within Taihoku Prefecture, taking in Bangka, Dadaocheng, the former walled city and smaller settlements.

milestones.title: Songshan annexed
milestones.detail: The eastern village of Matsuyama, today's Songshan and Xinyi districts, is annexed to Taihoku City as planned growth turns eastward.

milestones.title: Air raids and the end of Japanese rule
milestones.detail: Allied bombing damages government buildings, schools and houses in the old walled city. On 25 October 1945 Japanese forces in Taiwan surrender at Taipei City Hall.

milestones.title: Provisional capital of the Republic of China
milestones.detail: On 7 December 1949 the Kuomintang government makes Taipei its provisional capital. The arrival of people from the mainland sets off rapid growth in the 1950s.

milestones.title: Special municipality; six townships annexed
milestones.detail: Taipei becomes a centrally administered municipality on 1 July 1967. The next year it annexes Shilin, Beitou, Neihu, Nangang, Jingmei and Muzha.

milestones.title: Taipei Metro opens
milestones.detail: The first line of the Taipei Metro, a 10.5 km elevated line, opens on 28 March 1996.

milestones.title: Taipei 101 completed
milestones.detail: Taipei 101 is completed on 31 December 2004 and is the world's tallest building until 2009. Xinyi district becomes the city's main business centre.

notes: Scope: this file covers Taipei City's own history, which is the story of three adjoining settlements: Bangka (Mengjia, from 1709), Dadaocheng (from 1853) and the walled prefectural city built between them (1882-84), merged into one town after 1900. The UN series from 1950 treats Taipei together with its surrounding urban extent (today's New Taipei and beyond), so the pre-1950 city figures here are much smaller than the UN figure and there will be a step at 1950. Start date: 1709 is the date of the Chen Lai-chang land patent, generally taken as the beginning of Taipei's recorded history, and is not seriously contested. Before it the basin was Ketagalan land; the Spanish were active in northern Taiwan from the 1620s, but no town is recorded on the site. Population is thin: nothing was found before 1875 except a 19th-century remark that Bangka had 4,000-5,000 households and shops, which is recorded in a milestone, not as a population point. The 1875 figure is a modern scholar's estimate. Censuses of 1905, 1920 and 1935 are documented; the 1925, 1930 and 1940 census counts could not be traced to a census table, so 1925 is Chandler's rounded figure and 1940 and 1945 come from Taipei City Government statistics. Counts of the three towns around 1905 differ between sources (74,415 to over 86,000). Landmarks: pre-1900 coverage is weak. No sourced height was found for Lungshan Temple (1738), the surviving North Gate (1884), Bao'an Temple or the Confucius Temple, so they are left out; the city wall is included with an approximate height from a municipal teaching text and placed at the North Gate. The wall's demolished_year is the year demolition began.
